stated.value: Existing NIR pilot measuring API concentration at tablet press feed frame
One powder formulation with API and excipients
Introducing a different API and a different excipient blend
Reuse the existing NIR calibration for the new product
Add Raman so the old calibration remains valid
First technical assessment and first experiment

missing: Identity and chemistry of the new API, and its concentration range and target
Excipient composition of both blends and whether any excipient is shared
Current NIR calibration details: instrument model, wavelength range, pre-processing, PLS factors, RMSEP, reference method (e.g. HPLC) and validation data
Whether the old calibration failure is expected to be a bias, a slope change or a loss of selectivity
Raman hardware available (laser wavelength, power, probe type) and whether the feed frame has a suitable optical window or port
Feed frame geometry, powder flow and bulk density, and press speed or throughput
Acceptance limits for API content and the required measurement accuracy and precision
Regulatory context (GMP, PAT filing, validation requirements) and time available for the study

status_reason: The core question can be answered on principle: adding Raman does not preserve an NIR calibration. The new API and blend change the spectral basis of the model, so a new or updated calibration is needed regardless of the technique added. Specific chemistry, instrument and probe details are still missing and affect the plan.
answer: Adding Raman will not by itself keep the old calibration valid, because the calibration was built on NIR spectra of the old API and excipient blend and a new chemistry changes both the spectral response and the interferences. The first step should be a lab-first calibration-transfer study that tests how far the old NIR model fails on the new blend and builds a new or augmented calibration set, with Raman evaluated as a complementary method rather than a replacement for recalibration.

inline.headline: Treat this as a new calibration problem: test and rebuild in the lab before any in-line change at the feed frame
inline.method: Keep NIR as the main method for the existing pilot, since it is already installed and fast. Build a designed set of blended powders covering the new API and blend across the target concentration range, plus the old formulation as a control. Quantify the failure of the old model on the new blend, then test transfer approaches (bias or slope correction, or augmented PLS with the new samples). Evaluate Raman on the same samples as a complementary method if the new API has strong, selective Raman bands.
inline.probe: For NIR, reuse the existing feed frame probe and check that its window and geometry are unchanged. For Raman, a fiber-coupled non-contact probe with a focal distance suited to the feed frame, using a laser wavelength chosen to limit fluorescence from the excipients. Mount it on the same port as the NIR probe if the geometry allows, or on an adjacent port with the same sample view.
inline.install: Do not change the in-line installation until the lab study shows acceptable accuracy. Then install the Raman probe (if justified) on a short trial with no change to the press control loop, and log spectra alongside reference samples taken from the feed frame.
inline.fiber: Use low-fluorescence fiber for Raman, with a short run and a fiber bundle or single fiber matched to the probe. Keep the NIR fiber as it is. Verify the fiber length and connector losses in the lab before the trial, because the Raman signal is weak and sensitive to losses.
inline.test_against: A reference HPLC (or equivalent validated) assay of the API on the same blend samples, with the calibration set spanning the full concentration range and the old formulation as a control. Compare RMSEP, bias and slope for old model, transferred model, and new model on an independent validation set.
inline.not_final_because: The API identity, the existing calibration performance, the Raman hardware and the feed frame geometry are not known, and the choice between recalibration, transfer and Raman depends on the study results. The method and any in-line change must also be validated under the applicable GMP and PAT requirements before use.

problems.text: Adding Raman does not preserve the NIR calibration. A different API and excipient blend changes the spectral basis, so the NIR model built on the old formulation will not predict the new one reliably, whatever method is added alongside.
A new method has its own calibration. A Raman model cannot be assumed to transfer from NIR or from the old product, so Raman would also need its own calibration and validation on the new blend.

The NIR calibration may be transferable with a bias or slope correction if the new API has similar NIR bands and the excipients are similar. This must be shown by data, not assumed, which is why the lab study comes first.

Raman may suffer from fluorescence from excipients or the API, and the feed frame powder may give low signal or high background variability. The laser wavelength and the probe geometry must be checked before committing to Raman.

Sampling at the feed frame is a point measurement of a moving powder, so sampling error and the probe view may dominate the uncertainty. Probe position, powder density changes and window fouling must be considered in any in-line calibration.

Adding a second method increases the system complexity, the validation effort and the maintenance burden. Multivariate fusion of NIR and Raman may improve selectivity but also raises the risk of overfitting with a small calibration set.

methods.method: NIR (existing pilot) with recalibration or transfer
methods.why: Already installed at the feed frame and fast enough for in-line control. The first test is to quantify how well the old model predicts the new blend and whether bias or slope correction or augmented PLS restores accuracy.

Gives strong, specific bands for many APIs and is less sensitive to water and to some physical effects than NIR, so it may provide a selective second measurement. It needs its own calibration and suffers from fluorescence risk.
Worth considering only if neither method alone meets the accuracy target and both have useful selectivity. It adds complexity and requires a larger calibration set to avoid overfitting.

methods.method: Reusing the old NIR calibration unchanged
methods.why: Not supported for a new API and blend without demonstrated transfer on new samples, and it would expose the process to an uncontrolled prediction bias.

questions.q: What is the API, and does it have distinct NIR and Raman bands with low overlap with the excipients?
questions.why: The choice of method and the feasibility of transfer depend directly on the spectral selectivity of the new API.

questions.q: What is the concentration range of the API and the acceptance limits for the tablet?
questions.why: The calibration set must cover the range, and the required accuracy determines whether transfer or full recalibration is needed.

questions.q: How well does the existing NIR model perform on the old product (RMSEP, bias, slope, R2) and what reference method was used?
questions.why: The baseline performance sets the expected accuracy and shows whether the old model was robust or already marginal.

questions.q: Which excipients differ between the two blends, and are any of them strong NIR or Raman absorbers or fluorescent?
questions.why: Excipient changes are a common cause of calibration failure and of Raman fluorescence problems.

questions.q: What Raman hardware is available, including laser wavelength and probe options, and can a probe be mounted at the feed frame?
questions.why: Determines whether Raman is a practical option and what fluorescence risk and signal level to expect.

questions.q: What are the feed frame geometry, the window material and the powder flow and density characteristics?
questions.why: Affects probe view, sampling representativeness, window fouling and the ability to keep the same measurement geometry.

questions.q: What validation and regulatory requirements apply (GMP, PAT or other), and what is the time frame?
questions.why: Defines the evidence needed for a method change and the scope of the feasibility study.

experiment.objective: Determine whether the old NIR calibration can be transferred to the new API and blend, and whether Raman adds enough selective information to justify its use, using a lab-first study that precedes any change to the in-line installation.
steps: Confirm the API and excipient chemistry and obtain the spectra or reference spectra of pure API and each excipient for both blends.

Prepare a designed calibration set of blends at the new API across the target concentration range and at several levels of excipient variation, plus the old formulation as a control, with reference assay on each sample.
Collect NIR spectra of all samples using the existing instrument settings and record the old model prediction for each sample to quantify bias, slope and RMSEP on the new blend.
Test transfer options on the new data: bias or slope correction, direct standardization, and augmented PLS using a split of the new samples for calibration and an independent set for validation.
Collect Raman spectra of the same samples with a probe at the feed frame geometry if possible, check fluorescence and signal level, and build a Raman calibration with the same reference data.
If both methods are individually weak, test a combined NIR and Raman model on the same validation set and check for overfitting.
Run a short trial on the feed frame with reference sampling to confirm that the lab findings hold under real powder flow and probe geometry.
Document the results and decide on the calibration approach and whether Raman is worth installing.
references: Multivariate calibration and transfer literature for NIR (e.g. calibration transfer and standardization methods in pharmaceutical process analysis)
Process analytical technology guidance from regulators (e.g. FDA PAT guidance) for method validation and in-line measurement
Pharmacopoeial guidance on NIR and Raman identification and quantitative methods (e.g. USP and Ph. Eur. chapters on spectroscopic methods)
Literature on in-line Raman and NIR monitoring of tablet blends and powder feed
experiment.go_no_go: Go: the transferred or new model meets the accuracy target (for example RMSEP and bias within the acceptance limit for API content) on an independent validation set that includes the new blend, with no systematic bias at the concentration range edges, and the feed frame trial agrees with reference sampling. No-go: the transfer fails on the new blend or the required accuracy is not met even with recalibration, in which case the NIR model must be rebuilt entirely and the in-line use of the old model is withdrawn.

multispectral.combination: NIR as the main method with recalibration or transfer, plus Raman as a complementary method, and NIR and Raman data fusion considered only if each method alone is inadequate.
multispectral.why: NIR is already in place and fast, but its bands are broad and overlap between the old and new blends. Raman gives sharper, more specific bands for many APIs and is less affected by water, so it may provide a selective check on the NIR model. The combination is worth testing as a comparison, but it does not remove the need for new calibration data.

assumptions: The new API and excipients are chemically different enough that the old NIR model cannot be assumed to predict the new blend.
The feed frame measurement with the existing NIR probe is representative of the blend, and the powder sampling variance is small compared with the required accuracy.
A reference method such as HPLC is available and validated for the new API.
Raman can be installed at the feed frame with a suitable probe and window, though its feasibility is not yet confirmed.
The regulatory route allows a calibration update and method validation for the new product, and the existing NIR instrument can be used for the study.
